title: Hair dryer: safe teardown
summary: Many cheap hair dryers hold a small DC motor and impeller fed by a bridge rectifier from the heating element, a nichrome element on a mica former, a thermal cutout and slide switches. Once out, the motor can often run from a 6–12 V DC supply. Mains is the main danger, and dryers from the 1970s may hold asbestos.

steps.text: Unplug it, keep the plug where you can see it, and let it cool. Pull off the rear grille or lint filter.
Check its age. A dryer from the 1970s or earlier, salon dryers included, may have asbestos in its heat shield or liner. If it might be that old, leave it whole (see safety_asbestos_check).
steps.warn: Don't break, sand or blow out the insulation in an old dryer.

steps.text: Undo the screws in the handle and behind the grille. Most are Phillips; some need tri-wing or other security bits.
Split the two case halves. Work round the seam with a flat blade to free the snap-fit clips, slowly: the clips break.

Before you touch anything inside, look at the barrel and the heat shield round the element with the case still half open, and touch nothing. Grey, white or fibrous board, paper or lining there may be asbestos, and nobody can tell by sight. If you see any, or you are not sure, stop: close the case, take nothing out, and do not break, scrape, sand or blow dust off it. Choose another dryer (see safety_asbestos_check).

Look at how the inner assembly sits: motor and fan at the back, element in the barrel, switches in the handle. Photograph the wiring, but do not touch the wires or solder joints yet: the next step comes first.

Wait at least 5 minutes since you unplugged it. Some dryers have a small capacitor across the mains wires (iFixit hair dryer how it works). If you see one, discharge it with a resistor tool, then set the meter to DC volts and measure across it. It must read under 1 V before you touch the wiring. Never measure first (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
Now slide the inner assembly out in one piece. Hold it by the motor can or the barrel, not by the wires.

Find the bridge rectifier on the motor leads: a small black block with four legs, or four separate diodes. Mark which motor lead comes from its + leg. If there is no rectifier and the motor is marked AC, it is a mains motor: keep it for mains use only and skip the battery test.
Free the motor. Desolder or cut the two leads joining the motor and rectifier to the element, leaving long tails. Keep the rectifier with the motor.
steps.warn: A motor fed through a rectifier is a low-voltage motor. Never connect it, or its rectifier, straight to the mains.

steps.text: Leave the impeller on the motor shaft. On many dryers it is glued on and breaks if you force it.
Slide the element and its mica former out of the barrel or heat shield. Hold it by the mica, not the wire.
steps.warn: Mica cracks and the wire kinks. Don't flex the cards.

steps.text: Take the thermal cutout and any thermal fuse beside the element. Unclip them, or cut their leads as far from the body as you can. Never heat one to test it, and keep soldering heat away from its body.
Take the slide switches and cold-shot button from the handle, and cut the cord off at the case. Keep the big plug if it has test and reset buttons.

Test the motor: clamp or hold it so it cannot jump and keep fingers, hair and loose clothes clear of the impeller. Connect 6–12 V DC from a fused supply, + to the lead you marked. It should spin and blow air. Then test the other parts (see the notes).

notes:
## How the motor is fed

In many cheap dryers the fan motor is a small DC motor, not a mains motor. Mains current runs through the nichrome element, and part of the element (or a resistor) drops the voltage for the motor. A diode bridge turns that into DC. The Philips SalonDry Compact studied by iFixit runs on 230 V mains, with an RS-365S motor rated 12–17 V DC at about 20,000 rpm. In another circuit one element section is both a heater and the motor's voltage divider (iFixit hair dryer how it works). In use, the motor sees roughly 10 V (iFixit hair dryer failures). So never connect the motor, with or without its rectifier, straight to mains.

## What's worth keeping and why

- **Motor and impeller.** A small blower that runs from a battery. Uses: air for a charcoal stove or small forge (throttle it hard; see build_brake_drum_forge), a fan for a food dryer, or ventilation. Swap the battery leads and it runs backwards and blows less. Spun by hand with a meter on it, it shows whether it still works as a tiny generator.
- **Bridge rectifier.** Four diodes, often a small four-legged block on the motor leads. Small, low-current DC jobs only: polarity protection or a tiny generator.
- **Element.** Nichrome wire wound on a mica support (iFixit hair dryer how it works). Nichrome doesn't oxidise when heated (iFixit hair dryer how it works), so it is good spare wire for repairing a toaster or building a small heater. A short length on a low-voltage supply makes a hot-wire foam cutter: cut outdoors. Don't run a bare element on mains outside its dryer: it relies on the dryer's airflow and cutouts, and blocked air makes a dryer overheat (Conair 259 booklet).
- **Mica cards.** A heat-proof electrical insulator for winding your own small heater.
- **Thermal cutout and fuse.** A dryer's thermal cutout should be closed and should open only above about 100 °C (iFixit hair dryer failures). Whether it resets varies: the Dyson HD07 one does not (Dyson HD07 leaflet). A one-shot thermal fuse opens when its pellet melts and stays open (SCHOTT SEFUSE). A salvaged one is not proof of safety: see Reusing a thermal fuse below.
- **Switches.** Small mains slide switches, such as the TOPLY YSS-16 parts in the Revlon (iFixit Revlon 1875W).
- **Cord.** Light mains cord. In the US a hand-held dryer without built-in protection against water immersion counts as a substantial product hazard (CPSC hair dryer rule); the Conair 259 has a leakage interrupter (ALCI) in the big plug, with test and reset buttons, and its booklet says to run the test every time you use it (Conair 259 booklet). Keep the plug on the cord, test it each time, and do not trust one that fails the test.

## Variations

- **Revlon 1875W Compact.** Two Phillips #2 screws on the back of the handle, under the rear grille, and a snap-fit at the top hold the case. Inside are a DC motor marked yfd 385 with a 7-blade impeller glued to its shaft, two heating coils soldered close to the motor, and two slide switches (iFixit Revlon 1875W).
- **Revlon RVDR5061.** One long screw in the handle. The motor is soldered to the element assembly at two points, and the element joins a small board by four wires (iFixit Revlon RVDR5061).
- **Conair InfinitiPro 259.** 1,875 W on 110–125 V with an AC motor, an ALCI plug and an automatic overheat cutout (Conair 259 booklet). The booklet calls it an AC motor and says no more, so do not assume it will run from a battery; keep it for mains use.
- **Dyson Supersonic HD07 and other high-speed dryers.** The maker's leaflet warns that the dryer, filter and attachments contain magnets, tells users not to take it apart because wrong reassembly can cause shock or fire, and says its thermal cut-out does not reset by itself (Dyson HD07 leaflet).
- **Old dryers.** In 1979 the CPSC reported that UL had found asbestos heat-shield insulation in 25–40% of recently imported hand-held dryers (CPSC asbestos hair dryers). In 1980 it announced a recall of more than 87,000 further dryers, mostly professional salon models, with asbestos liners or heat shields (CPSC 1980 asbestos recall). Nobody can tell asbestos by sight: if the heat shield or liner is grey, fibrous or crumbling, leave the dryer whole.

## Testing what you got out

Test parts out of the dryer, or with one wire taken off (see test_continuity).

- **Element.** Set the meter to ohms. The whole element should read about volts × volts ÷ watts: 120 V, 1,875 W is about 7.7 Ω, and 230 V, 2,000 W about 26 Ω. Separate sections read more; iFixit found a few tens of ohms each on a 230 V dryer (iFixit hair dryer failures). OL means a break. Test from each terminal to any metal part: it must read OL.
- **Thermal cutout and fuse.** One that has not opened reads close to 0 Ω, and OL means it has opened or is broken. That is all the meter shows: a reading near 0 Ω does not prove a salvaged cutout or fuse will still open at its rating (SCHOTT SEFUSE). Never heat one to test it.
- **Bridge rectifier.** Set the meter to diode test. Each of the four diodes should read about 0.5–0.7 V one way and OL the other. A short either way means it is dead. Diodes are a common failure: a motor that won't turn, or only crawls, often has one gone (iFixit hair dryer failures).
- **Motor.** Connect 6–12 V DC, + to the lead you marked. It should spin and blow air. If it is stiff, pull hair and fluff off the shaft (iFixit hair dryer failures).
- **Switches and cord.** Test each switch position for continuity. Test each cord wire end to end while you bend the cord: breaks are common at the plug and where it enters the handle (iFixit hair dryer failures).

## Reusing a thermal fuse

Treat a salvaged thermal fuse or cutout as unproven. A meter shows only that it is closed. SCHOTT says a thermal link can be changed by mechanical load or heat while it is handled or mounted, that long exposure near its holding temperature shrinks the pellet for good, and that soldering heat can make one open (SCHOTT SEFUSE). A fuse out of an old dryer may have had all of that.

- Never heat one to test it.
- Never bridge a fuse or cutout with wire, and never leave one out.
- Never make a salvaged one the only protection against overheating in anything you build. Use a new part of known rating, and add a salvaged one, if at all, only as an extra.
- A thermal link is not a current fuse (SCHOTT SEFUSE): the supply needs its own fuse as well.
- If you fit one anyway, match its temperature rating and keep it below its rated volts and amps. Join it by crimping, welding or soldering at least 5 mm from the body, gripping the lead with pliers between the joint and the body and soldering in short bursts. Bend leads at least 3 mm from the body (SCHOTT SEFUSE).

## What to leave

- A dryer old enough to have asbestos: leave the heat shield whole (see safety_asbestos_check).
- Dyson and other high-speed dryers.
- The ioniser in an ionic model (the Conair 259 and Dyson sheets list one): no source gives its voltage, so leave it in the dryer.
- A glued impeller: leave it on the motor.
- Kinked or brittle element wire and cracked mica.
